title: The Beloved Gaius
subtitle: 3 John 1:1–4
description: The elder's one letter to a named friend: the beloved Gaius, prayed for in body as his soul prospers, and praised on the brothers' testimony for walking in the truth.
paragraphs: Of all the elder's letters, this is the only one addressed to a friend by name: “The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth:” The signature is the same title as the letter before it, no name, only the elder. But the address has changed key. The chosen lady of the last letter was greeted with her household; Gaius is greeted as a man, beloved, and loved in the truth, the same located love as before, here resting on one person. Everything this page will say, praise, warning, and commendation, is said inside a friendship, and the friendship is not decoration on the letter; it is the letter's whole method.

The first thing the friendship does is pray, and it prays for the body: “Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers.” Notice the sentence's balance. The soul's prospering is stated as the known fact, reported and sure: your soul also prospers, the also placing the man's inner life first in order of certainty. The health and the prospering in every way are prayed for, desired aloud by a friend who treats a man's body and his circumstances as worthy subjects of prayer. The telling builds no system on the verse; it stands as what it is, one elder's real prayer for one friend's health, and a window into what the elder already knew about Gaius before he asked for anything.

What he knew had come to him by report, and the report is the letter's second movement: “For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk.” The brothers are the letter's couriers, traveling men whose road runs between the elder and Gaius, and their testimony about him is of a piece: devotion to the truth and a walk that continues in it. Overjoyed is the elder's word for Gaius exactly as it was for the lady's children in the letter before. In both letters the elder's joy is never abstract; it always has a report behind it and feet under it, somebody found walking.

The joy rises in the next verse into the nearest thing this writer has to a personal motto: “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.” My children: the elder counts the believers of these households as his own, and his scale of joys is stated as a superlative, no greater joy than this one. Not conversions counted, not churches planted, not opponents answered; hearing that his children walk in the truth outranks every other report that could reach an old man's ears. The verse explains the whole page that follows, because the letter will now divide its world by exactly that walk: those who receive the walking brothers, and one man who drives them away.

Two plain statements belong here, once. The elder never names himself; tradition has long ascribed the letter to John the apostle, named here as tradition, with the letter's authority left on the elder's own voice. And Gaius is not identified beyond this page: the New Testament names more than one man called Gaius, and this letter gives no way to tell whether its friend is any of them, so no biography is built for him. The book stands in the undated group of this series, with no date given and none invented. What the page does give is about to widen: Gaius's house has been open to strangers, and the elder is ready to praise the open door by name.

title: Send Them On Their Way
subtitle: 3 John 1:5–8
description: Hospitality praised and defined: faithfulness to brothers who are strangers, travelers sent on in a manner worthy of God, and supporters named fellow workers for the truth.
paragraphs: The praise gets specific, and its measure is hospitality: “Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you.” Faithful is the word chosen, not generous or kind, as if receiving the traveling brothers were a trust to be kept. And the detail the elder lingers on is that they are strangers to you: Gaius did not open his house to friends repaying friendship, but to men whose only claim on him was the work they carried. In a world where the faith moved on foot from household to household, a stranger's knock was the mission arriving, and Gaius's answer to it had become the thing the brothers talked about.

They talked about it formally: “They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God.” Testified to the church: the same witness language the elder uses for the truth itself, here spent on one host's love, reported in public because it deserved a record. And the instruction that follows raises the standard past decency: send them on in a manner worthy of God, provisions and honor measured not by what travelers usually get but by the God they travel for. The guest's worth is set by his Sender, and the host who grasps that gives accordingly.

The reason the support system falls on households is stated in one sentence: “For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles.” On behalf of the Name, the elder's title for the cause, the name of Jesus carried without the name being spelled. And they accept nothing from those outside: the travelers will not take support from the world they are sent to, which means the whole weight of the road rests on the houses of the faith. A closed door is therefore not a private choice in this letter's world; it is a break in the supply line of the Name itself.

So the elder draws the conclusion as a duty shared: “Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.” Ought, and we, the elder counting himself among the supporters, and the dignity he gives the support is the episode's crown: the host who feeds and forwards a traveler becomes a fellow worker for the truth, a partner in work he never leaves home to do. This is the open door of the elder's world, the exact counterpart to the shut door of the letter before it, where a household was told to refuse the teacher who denies the confession. Both doors are the same elder's teaching in two settings. What this letter adds is a grief: somewhere in Gaius's own church, a door is being shut from the inside, by a man whose name the elder is about to say out loud.

title: Do Not Imitate Evil
subtitle: 3 John 1:9–14
description: Diotrephes, who loves to be first, refuses the brothers and expels the willing; the rule is to imitate good, not evil; Demetrius is commended; and the letter closes with greetings by name.
paragraphs: The shadow has a name and the elder does not protect it: “I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction.” A letter to the church exists behind this one, unseen by us, and its fate tells the story: the man in the way loves to be first, the one motive the text itself assigns him, and out of that love he will not accept the elder's instruction. The telling invents no deeper wound or history for him. First is the whole diagnosis the elder gives, a man for whom the church's door and the church's welcome have become instruments of his own rank.

What the rank produces is then listed, item by item: “So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us.” “And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church.” The elder's remedy is stated as intent only, if I come, I will call attention, and no visit or confrontation is invented beyond his words. The acts stand as he lists them: slander against the elder himself, the brothers refused at the door, the willing forbidden, and the extraordinary last step, members put out of the church for the crime of wanting to welcome. Gaius's open house and Diotrephes's closed church are the same test from opposite sides, and the expelled members are what loving first place costs a congregation.

Against the portrait the elder sets the rule, addressed to his friend as a safeguard rather than an accusation: “Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God.” Two examples now stand on the page, the host and the first-loved man, and imitation is the elder's frame for both: a person becomes what he copies. The second half stands at the strength he states it, doing good as the mark of being of God, evil-doing as the mark of a man who has not seen God, the letter's own test for reading the two portraits, carried as he gives it and aimed at no one beyond the page.

Then, deliberately, a third name, set down as the opposite record: “Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true.” Three witnesses stack: everyone who knows him, the truth itself as if it were a character witness, and the elder's own we, vouched for by Gaius's knowledge of its honesty. Whether Demetrius carries this very letter the page does not say, and the telling leaves it open; what the page does is give Gaius a man worth imitating by name, so the rule of the last paragraph has a face as well as the warning has.

The letter ends as its sister letter did, with the pen set down: “I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink.” “Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face. Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name.” Face to face is stated as hope, and no visit is invented past it. Peace to you is the elder's benediction over a friend caught between an open house and a closing church, and the last instruction keeps the smallest kindness in the whole letter: greet them by name, each one known. The elder's page closes there, and one book remains in the undated group, a short letter with fire in it from a man who calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James: Jude.
